body.text: In short:
The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates to a 15-year high as the Middle East oil shock adds to inflation pressures that were already building in Australia.
The decision has fuelled scrutiny of government spending, weak productivity and the economy's capacity to meet demand.
What's next?
The Coalition is pressing Labor over its economic management as borrowers absorb what is the fourth rate rise this year.
Another interest rate rise has intensified pressure on Labor to tackle the domestic problems that were driving high inflation before the Middle East war sparked the global oil shock.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has defended the federal government's economic record while attributing higher prices in Australia to the ongoing Iran conflict and AI investment boom, though he conceded those were not the only factors.

Household borrowers already struggling with the cost of living are under more pressure after the Reserve Bank unanimously voted to increase the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.6 per cent on Tuesday.
The Coalition has seized on the hike, which brought rates to their highest level in 15 years, to argue government spending was the "major culprit".

Mr Chalmers said he accepted "responsibility for my part in the fight against inflation" but argued the US war with Iran had "turbocharged" fuel costs and that Australians were paying a "very hefty price" for it.
Reserve Bank Governor Michelle Bullock said she would not "play the blame game" but her diagnosis was broader than Mr Chalmers's repeated emphasis on the war.
She said inflation had been "driven by domestic capacity pressures" and that the oil shock came "in addition to this".
"This isn't all about the Middle East conflict," Ms Bullock said.
"It is making things much worse, but we did start from a position of excess demand anyway, and that's why we started raising interest rates even before the conflict started."

The distinction has left the government under pressure over the parts of the inflation problem within its control, particularly spending, productivity and the economy's capacity to accommodate demand for goods and services.
Labor's spending under fire
Speaking after the rate rise, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government was spending "too much" and argued the economy was "not working".
"Households, families are having to tighten their belts, but the government hasn't tightened its belt," he said.

Figures released this week showed government spending reached 26.9 per cent of gross domestic product last financial year, which was the highest level, aside from during the pandemic, in four decades.
At the same the total tax take climbed to 24.1 per cent, which was just shy of the Howard government-era record.

Mr Chalmers argued the headline spending figured obscured a significant slowdown in public demand, noting that four out of every five dollars of demand added to the economy over the last year had come from the private sector.

He also said the changes in the federal budget, in particular a "productivity package" and efforts to "repair" the bottom line through NDIS changes, showed the government was taking the inflation challenge "very seriously".
Ms Bullock said the public and private sectors did add to aggregate demand though insisted there was not any "particular" items making the RBA's job "harder".
Demand for goods and services, driven in part by the AI investment boom, has grown faster than businesses can supply them which has pushed up prices.
Stronger productivity would allow more to be produced without adding to inflation, but Ms Bullock was blunt in her assessment of progress on this.
"The bottom line is that productivity is doing nothing,"

Ms Bullock said the ongoing Iran war suggested higher costs would persist for "longer than previously expected" and warned businesses would raise their prices to view the disruption as a longer term issue.
RBA understands household pain, Bullock says
The rate hike, which was the fourth this year, will add about $91 to the monthly repayments of a typical home owner with a 25 year $600,000 mortgage.

Markets are also not ruling out another increase when the RBA meets next in November, with new Consumer Price Index figures due to be released on Wednesday expected to show a jump in inflation due to higher fuel prices.

Pushed to justify the impact of rate rises on Australians who have no control over many of the factors driving inflation, Ms Bullock said people would be feeling "quite rightly very annoyed and upset" about rising costs.
"They are seeing … real wage cuts and then, on top of that, they have got this shock from the Middle East which is nothing to do with them, but it's made us all poorer," she said.
Ms Bullock said she understood those "sentiments" but maintained the "best thing" the RBA could do was get inflation down to between two and three per cent where it "sits in the background".
"When we can get to that point … and hopefully if we get some productivity growth, then we'll be able to grow and we will be able to get some real wage rises," she said.
Mr Chalmers said the government knew Australians were "under pressure", which was why it was providing cost-of-living help "in the most responsible way we can".
